Consider a 62-year-old with $1 million in a 401(k) who has never bought a single share of Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA). That saver owns Nvidia anyway: about $50,000 of it if the money sits in an S&P 500 index fund, and roughly $14,000 if it sits in a 2030 target-date fund. Nvidia closed Friday at $125.53, 47.5% below its Oct. 6 record close of $239.24. The stock lost nearly half its value in six weeks, and if you hold either kind of fund in your own 401(k), a slice of that loss is yours. The fund figures here come from 24/7 Wall St.’s new research report, "Nvidia Without Jensen," which traced Nvidia through the holdings that fund companies publish and file. Is NVIDIA a Buy After Jensen Huang's Departure? Plus 3 New Buys and the RSI Race Heats Up Nvidia’s fall reads as a warning to check how much of your 401(k) rides on a handful of giant stocks, because seven companies make up 32.5% of the S&P 500 fund; the limit of that reading is that the same fund fell 11.5% while one of its biggest stocks lost nearly half its value. Nvidia was 5.7% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF on Nov. 19, the day before Friday’s 14% drop, according to State Street Global Advisors’ daily holdings. Only Apple, at 8.2%, and Microsoft, at 6%, were bigger. An S&P 500 index fund on a 401(k) menu tracks the same index, so its weights are close to these. Friday’s drop cut that weight. Adjusting the Nov. 19 holdings for Friday’s closing prices, Nvidia ended the week at about 5.1% of the fund. On the saver’s balance, that is about $50,000. The larger number sits beside it. Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Tesla together were 32.5% of the fund on Nov. 19, according to the same holdings. That was $325,000 of the account in seven companies, inside a fund that holds about 500. The past six weeks show what that concentration does. The SPDR fund closed Friday 11.5% below its Oct. 6 close. Working back from the Nov. 19 weight and the two price changes, Nvidia was about 8.6% of the fund on Oct. 6, and its fall accounts for about 4.1 of the fund’s 11.5 points. That is 36% of the whole decline, from one stock. In dollars, $1 million in the fund at the Oct. 6 close was worth $885,405 at Friday’s close. About $41,000 of the roughly $115,000 lost came from Nvidia. Friday’s drop closed out what I reported was Nvidia’s worst week since 2008. A target-date fund owns stock funds and bond funds, and it shifts toward bonds as its year gets closer. That shift decides how much Nvidia you own. Vanguard’s filings with the SEC for June 30 show its Target Retirement 2050 Fund kept about 54% of its money in Vanguard’s total U.S. stock market fund, and Nvidia was about 6.4% of that fund. Multiply the two, and a $100,000 balance in the 2050 fund held about $3,412 of Nvidia, or 3.4%. The 2030 fund, the one built for a 62-year-old who plans to stop work at about 66, held about 2.2% in Nvidia. By our calculation from the same filings, it kept roughly 35% of its money in that stock fund and more in bonds. On the saver’s balance, that was $22,000 of Nvidia. Nvidia closed at $200.09 on June 30. At Friday’s price the same shares are worth about $13,800, the roughly $14,000 in the first paragraph. At the Oct. 6 record they were worth about $26,300. The fall from the record cost this saver about $12,500, a little over 1% of the account. The June filings are the latest on file, so this is an estimate that assumes the fund still holds the same shares. Other companies’ target-date funds will differ a little. The saver in this example has a decision coming. Many people roll a 401(k) into an IRA when they retire and pick new funds. Moving the whole balance from the 2030 target-date fund to an S&P 500 index fund would lift the Nvidia stake from roughly $14,000 to about $50,000, more than three times as much. It would also put nearly a third of the money in seven companies. You can run the same check on your own account in a few minutes. Find each fund’s top 10 holdings on its fact sheet or your plan’s website. Multiply your balance in each fund by Nvidia’s weight and add the results. An S&P 500 fund and a Nasdaq-100 fund held together stack up, since Nvidia was 6.1% of the Nasdaq-100 on Nov. 19, according to Global X’s holdings of those stocks. Then do the same for the seven largest companies, and add any single stocks you hold outside the plan. To skip the math, we’re putting Nvidia’s share of the most common target-date and S&P 500 index funds in The Daily Profit, our free weekday email. Get it here and check your own funds in a minute. My read of these numbers is that Nvidia’s fall is a reason to count what you own. For the saver in the 2030 fund, a stock that lost nearly half its value cost a little over 1% of the account, and selling a broad fund after a drop would lock that loss in. Continue » The macro environment for Nvidia is similarly bullish. Research from Apollo Global Management (NYSE:APO) says: Historically, technology shortages have typically been traced to a single chokepoint. What makes the current environment unusual is that constraints are appearing across many layers of the supply chain at once. The most obvious shortage remains deployed GPUs. On-demand GPU capacity is effectively sold out, and even older-generation chips are seeing rental rates increase to levels not seen since 2024. Hyperscalers and model builders continue to spend aggressively to secure supply, in some cases signing multiyear infrastructure commitments well ahead of deployment. What, then, is dragging down Nvidia stock? There are three main culprits. First, the company is dealing with the ongoing fallout of CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The company could face regulatory blowback, export restrictions, and weaker long-term leadership following Huang's exit. Second, reporting suggests that Nvidia engaged in a form of circular financing, injecting cash into artificial intelligence (AI) start-ups to absorb excess GPU supply. Third, investors are concerned about potential margin compression as both hyperscalers and other GPU producers invest aggressively to scale their own chip production. But here's the thing: If you commit to a 20-year holding period, few of these current concerns will ultimately matter. Normally, it is difficult to forecast a company's next couple of decades. Nvidia's situation is surprisingly straightforward. While the company's dominant market share in AI GPUs is driven by long-term planning and software ecosystem investment, sales growth is largely driven by industrywide demand. In other words, Nvidia is a high-quality boat in a tide that will rise for decades to come. "Nvidia has a wide economic moat," asserts research from Morningstar. How quickly is that AI market growing, and how long will it sustain those growth rates? "A massive wave of data center construction will have implications through 2050," stresses research from PwC. "The AI infrastructure cycle underway will likely dwarf previous investment booms in areas like railways, electrification, or the internet." In no scenario does PwC forecast data center spending to fall under $20 trillion by 2050. "Across all three scenarios, capex rises significantly through 2050," the firm predicts. Compounding double-digit annual sales growth -- which should persist over the next two decades -- should more than offset margin normalization, especially considering the next few years should still generate industry-leading profitability. A 64-year-old retired accountant with an $800,000 IRA has kept $40,000 of it in cash since 2020, waiting for Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) stock to get cheaper. On Friday Nvidia closed at $125.53, 48% below the record it set on Oct. 6, and it now trades at 15 times its earnings of the last four quarters. That is the lowest price-to-earnings ratio Nvidia has had since at least 2014. The accountant is an example. If you also passed on Nvidia because it looked too expensive, the stock has not been this cheap on that measure in more than a decade. Since January 2014 its median price-to-earnings ratio has been 45. At the October record, six weeks ago, it was 34. Is Now The Time To Buy For Alphabet, Microsoft or Nvidia? My reading is that a price this low assumes Nvidia’s profit growth is nearly over. The limit of that reading is that a price-to-earnings ratio is only as good as the earnings in it, and investors have two new reasons to question Nvidia’s: the board accepted co-founder Jensen Huang’s resignation as chief executive on Nov. 11 and has not named a permanent successor, and Reuters reported on Friday that Securities and Exchange Commission staff are examining its accounting. The figures come from “Nvidia Without Jensen,” a new research report from 24/7 Wall St. The measure is the share price divided by adjusted earnings per share for the last four reported quarters, which add up to $8.39. The report checked it at the end of every month from January 2014 through Friday, using Nasdaq closing prices adjusted for splits and the earnings in Nvidia’s quarterly releases. The ratio fell because the price dropped while earnings rose. At the October record, the last four quarters of adjusted earnings came to $7.01 a share. Nvidia reported another quarter on Nov. 17, and the total is now 20% higher. Over the same six weeks the share price fell from $239.24 to $125.53. The retired accountant had good reason to wait. From 2020 through this September, the ratio ended a month below 30 only once. The forward price-to-earnings ratio divides the share price by what analysts expect a company to earn in its next fiscal year. It rests on estimates, so it is softer than a ratio built on reported results. At Friday’s close Nvidia traded at 8.2 times forward earnings. Broadcom traded at 16.5 times, Meta Platforms at 16.8, Alphabet at 18.4 and Microsoft at 24.5. Amazon and Advanced Micro Devices were both above 20. Every one of those companies grew sales more slowly than Nvidia did in its latest quarter. Microsoft and Broadcom also cost more than Nvidia on the reported earnings of their last four quarters, at about 25 and 39 times. Of the eight companies the report compared, only Micron Technology was lower, at less than 4 times forward earnings. Memory chips are a boom-and-bust business, and my reading of a forward ratio that low is that investors expect the forecast profits to fade. At 8.2 times, the market is applying some of the same doubt to Nvidia. Suppose the accountant wants that $40,000 to earn 10% a year. In five years it has to be worth about $64,400. Here is what that takes from Nvidia. The 10% return and the future ratio of 20 are our assumptions, picked to be modest, and you can swap in your own. Its net income for the last four quarters was $226 billion under standard accounting rules, according to its filings with the SEC. So the price needs profit to grow 7.9% in five years, about 1.5% a year. In the past year that profit more than doubled. If the stock still trades at 15 times earnings in 2031, the same return takes $325 billion of yearly profit, 44% more than today’s. Nothing in Nvidia’s latest report shows growth stopping. Revenue has risen for eight straight quarters, from $39.3 billion to $115.8 billion, and was up 103% from a year earlier in the quarter that ended Oct. 25. The company’s outlook for the current quarter is $130 billion. The doubt comes from three things a ratio cannot measure. So Nvidia is cheap on the numbers, and the numbers are what investors are questioning. In my view, buying at this price is a bet that the reported profits are sound and that the next chief executive keeps the biggest customers buying. If you waited years for a lower price, three pieces of news matter more than the ratio now: the name of the permanent CEO, whatever Nvidia or the SEC says about the inquiry, and the customer percentages in the next quarterly report. We’ll flag each of those three the morning it lands in The Daily Profit, along with what Eric Bleeker, who runs our $1 million AI portfolio, does about it. It comes free here. Until then, size the purchase for the chance that the doubters are right. The accountant’s $40,000 is 5% of the IRA. If Nvidia’s earnings shrink and the stock falls by half again, the loss is $20,000, or 2.5% of the account. US securities regulators are investigating the accounting practices of Nvidia, according to US media, adding to the turmoil engulfing the artificial intelligence chip giant following the resignation of its chief executive. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) inquiry is in its early stages, The New York Times reported Saturday, citing people briefed on the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal reported on the investigation earlier this week, although it was unable to establish its precise focus. The probe could end without any charges being brought against the company. Questions about Nvidia's financial disclosures have intensified amid scrutiny of its dealings with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company investigated by American authorities over suspected shipments of restricted AI chips to China. Nvidia last year changed how it reported sales by geographical location, switching from customers' billing addresses to the countries where they are headquartered, US media reported. The change removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown, despite the company's significant business there. It remains unclear whether the SEC investigation is connected to those accounting changes or to the scandal surrounding former chief executive Jensen Huang. Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive suspected by US intelligence of working for Beijing. China has denied the espionage allegations, while Megaspeed has maintained that it operates lawfully. Nvidia's board has appointed former chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Huang's departure. The upheaval has shaken investor confidence in one of the world's most valuable companies, whose advanced semiconductors have been central to the global AI boom. Nvidia shares plunged 14 percent on Friday, bringing their losses for the week to more than 20 percent. US President Donald Trump nevertheless called Friday for Huang to be reinstated. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," Trump told reporters. But Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones has ruled out his return, saying board directors unanimously accepted his resignation. Tip: Try a valid symbol or a specific company name for relevant results

On Nov. 12, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) founder and chief executive officer Jensen Huang resigned from his post after a series of extramarital affairs (including one with an alleged Chinese spy) came to light. To make matters worse, the U.S. government is now investigating some of the company's customers in Southeast Asia to determine whether advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips were illegally forwarded to businesses in China. Nvidia stock has plummeted by 37% from its peak amid the turmoil, and it's now trading at the cheapest valuation in a decade. However, the company just reported a blockbuster set of operating results for its fiscal 2027 third quarter (ended Oct. 25), and interim CEO Colette Kress even issued a higher revenue forecast for the upcoming 2028 fiscal year. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » As a result, while Nvidia's challenges are likely to cause further short-term volatility in its stock, I think its booming business and solid fundamentals will ultimately prevail. Here's where I predict the stock will be trading in one year. Nvidia has come a long way since launching its first dedicated AI graphics processing unit (GPU) for the data center, the Hopper-based H100, in 2022. It went on to release the Blackwell and Blackwell Ultra architectures in 2024 and 2025, the latter of which can deliver up to 50 times more output performance than Hopper. But Nvidia started shipping its new Vera Rubin systems during the recent third quarter, which include the Rubin GPU, Vera central processing unit (CPU), and a series of upgraded networking components. It can deliver up to 30 times the performance of the equivalent Blackwell Ultra system, translating into a potential 97% reduction in inference token costs. Inference tokens are the text, images, or computer code generated by an AI model in response to a prompt, so Vera Rubin could significantly reduce the cost of running AI software. This is likely to drive greater AI adoption while making data center operators more profitable, fueling further demand for Nvidia's chips. Colette Kress said Vera Rubin achieved almost $20 billion in sales during the third quarter alone, making this the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history. Nvidia generated a record $115.8 billion in revenue during the third quarter, a whopping 103% increase from the year-ago period. The data center segment alone accounted for $107.6 billion of that total, and it grew at an even faster pace of 110%. Nvidia's physical AI business also deserves a mention. It develops the hardware and software technologies required to run robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial systems, and more, and its revenue more than tripled year over year during the third quarter. It's now on track to generate $25 billion in total sales for the current fiscal year (which ends on Jan. 31, 2027), so it could soon become a key source of growth for the entire company. Kress also said Nvidia could deliver $130 billion in total revenue during the fourth quarter, exceeding Wall Street's consensus expectation of $125.1 billion. Plus, she told investors that revenue could grow by 75% during fiscal 2028, upping the company's original forecast of 70% from a few months ago. That was a very positive surprise, and it dispels some of the speculation that Nvidia's sales will take a major hit amid any potential investigations into its dealings with customers in Southeast Asia. Jensen Huang and Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, are expected to testify before Congress in early December, where they will be questioned about potential national security breaches involving the prohibited sale of advanced AI chips to China. It's difficult to know what will come of these hearings, but I think investors are now being compensated for the potential risks because of Nvidia's rock-bottom valuation. Nvidia stock is trading at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of just 16.2 as I write this on Nov. 19, which is a fraction of its 10-year average of 61.1. It's also the lowest valuation in a decade. Moreover, Wall Street still believes Nvidia will grow its earnings to $16.61 per share in fiscal 2028, placing its forward P/E ratio at just 9.1. For some perspective, that's less than half the forward P/E of the Nasdaq-100 index, which is 20.7, so Nvidia looks extremely undervalued compared to a collective of America's leading technology giants. As a result, I think there is room for Nvidia stock to trade significantly higher over the next 12 months, provided the company's fiscal 2028 guidance remains intact and isn't disrupted by a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending, a loss of market share, or government investigations. These are genuine risks, but Kress's decision to raise the forecast suggests the sales pipeline is robust enough to weather them. Even if Nvidia stock doubles over the next year, it will still be cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 on a P/E basis, so I feel confident predicting a price of at least $200. But I think there is a real chance the stock reclaims its previous high of $239. Wall Street is sharply divided—with analysts pointing to a clash between some of the strongest earnings growth in corporate history and one of the most severe leadership, regulatory, and market crises Silicon Valley has ever seen. Shares of Nvidia (NVDA) closed at $125.53 on Friday, November 20, 2026, plunging 14.01% on the day to extend a seven-week losing streak. Since hitting a record 52-week high of $243.37 on October 6, the AI chip giant has shed more than $2.7 trillion in market value—nearly $900 billion of it wiped out during this week’s sell-off alone. Nvidia’s slide is the product of an extraordinary pileup of company-specific shocks hitting at the exact moment Wall Street’s broader AI trade began to buckle: Despite the panic, several fundamental and technical factors keep a recovery—or at least a sharp bounce—firmly on the table: Bears argue that the current sell-off is not a temporary dip, but the start of a longer structural reset for both Nvidia and the AI economy: Speculation over Huang’s next act has already become a sideshow for NVDA traders. At a White House briefing Friday, President Donald Trump publicly defended Huang, saying, "I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," and suggesting Nvidia accept his apology and reinstate him. Elon Musk and Uber founder Travis Kalanick have also backed a petition calling for Huang’s return, while Musk replied on X that hiring Huang at SpaceX "would be an honor." Huang remains Nvidia’s largest individual shareholder, holding a stake still worth roughly $102 billion at Friday’s close. On prediction market Polymarket, however, bettors currently see starting his own company as the most likely next move (27%), followed by taking no new formal job before 2028 (24%), with a return to Nvidia trailing at 20%. Over the coming weeks, Nvidia’s trajectory will hinge less on valuation models and more on hard answers—starting with Huang’s December 1 congressional appearance, the board’s response to Treasury and SEC inquiries, and how quickly the company can stabilize its leadership and defend its margins. title: Nvidia (NVDA) shares fell sharply as SEC investigates potential accounting issues - Beinsure
content: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) shares fell sharply after reports that the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating potential accounting issues at the AI chipmaker, adding to a series of legal and regulatory problems that have erased approximately $1 tn from its market capitalization in a week. SEC enforcement staff are examining the company’s accounting practices, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the confidential investigation. The Wall Street Journal had previously disclosed the existence of an SEC inquiry without identifying its focus. The investigation contributed to another sell-off on Friday, November 20. Nvidia shares fell approximately 14% during the session, extending their weekly decline to 23%, the company’s worst weekly performance since October 2008. The stock had already been under pressure following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang and allegations involving his relationship with a woman suspected by US authorities of working for Chinese intelligence. Strong quarterly earnings reported Tuesday failed to reverse the decline. The SEC declined to comment on its investigation, while Nvidia representatives did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Neither the specific accounting matters under examination nor the date the inquiry began has been established publicly. An SEC investigation does not constitute evidence of wrongdoing and may conclude without enforcement action. The investigation has renewed attention on Nvidia’s geographic revenue reporting, particularly its treatment of sales associated with Singapore. In 2025, Nvidia changed its method for reporting revenue by geographic location, replacing customer billing addresses with customer headquarters. The company said the revised approach provided a more accurate representation of the geographical distribution of its business. The change removed Singapore as a separate category in Nvidia’s geographic revenue breakdown. The Financial Times reported that Nvidia introduced the revised methodology even as sales attributed to Singapore had increased to almost half of global revenue under the previous reporting approach. The distinction between billing locations, customer headquarters and final destinations of semiconductor products has become a concern because of US restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China. Nvidia reported $19.7 bn in revenue from customers headquartered in China during fiscal 2026. That figure does not establish whether any products were shipped or transferred in violation of US export controls. The SEC has not publicly indicated whether geographic revenue reporting is part of its investigation. Suggestions that the inquiry involves Singapore-related sales or the ultimate destination of Nvidia chips remain speculative. Nvidia is also facing scrutiny over its historical business relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company previously led by Alice Huang. US authorities suspect Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence, an allegation denied by China. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a November 8 statement following reports about his relationship with Alice Huang, although he did not identify her by name. Megaspeed has historically been a major purchaser of Nvidia processors. US authorities have investigated the company since 2024 over possible violations of semiconductor export restrictions involving alleged shipments of advanced AI chips to China. The US Justice and Commerce departments confirmed the investigations during the week. Megaspeed said Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and maintained that its business operations were lawful. Reuters has been unable to contact Alice Huang for comment. The investigations follow years of US restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports to China, introduced in 2022 over concerns that the technology could strengthen Beijing’s military capabilities. Southeast Asia has attracted particular attention because of the possibility that intermediaries could obtain restricted chips for Chinese customers. According to reports about the Megaspeed investigation, a US Commerce Department official discovered Nvidia equipment still packaged at a Malaysian data center site in 2024, raising questions about whether the hardware was intended for onward shipment. The allegations have increased political scrutiny of Nvidia’s business relationships and its compliance with US export regulations. Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify behind closed doors on December 1 before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence Committee. A transcript of the proceedings could subsequently be released. The SEC accounting inquiry is separate from an ongoing Justice Department examination of Nvidia’s acquisition activities and commercial practices. Reuters reported in October that the Justice Department was reviewing Nvidia’s $12.9 bn agreement to acquire open-source AI platform Hugging Face. That review forms part of a broader antitrust investigation into Nvidia’s acquisitions and business conduct. The company consequently faces several distinct areas of regulatory scrutiny, including potential accounting issues, semiconductor export controls and competition concerns. No public information establishes that these investigations concern the same conduct or will result in enforcement action. Nvidia’s financial relationships with AI companies and cloud infrastructure providers have also drawn attention from analysts and investors. Chipmakers have participated in financing arrangements that help customers purchase processors and develop data centers. Nvidia has invested in AI businesses, supported cloud providers and provided guarantees associated with infrastructure projects using its equipment. Critics argue that such arrangements can complicate assessments of revenue quality and the financial risks companies retain through their relationships with customers. One concern involves circular financing, where capital supplied to an AI company or infrastructure provider can ultimately support purchases of equipment from the investor or its business partners. These transactions are not inherently improper, but their structure and disclosure can affect investors’ understanding of commercial demand and financial exposure. SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock told in October that the regulator was reviewing corporate disclosures by AI companies to determine whether investors were receiving adequate information about potential risks. During Nvidia’s Tuesday earnings call, interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress defended the company’s role in supporting AI industry development but said it would become substantially more selective about future financing agreements. The company has not publicly connected that policy change to the SEC investigation. The investigation comes as the SEC under President Donald Trump has shifted its enforcement priorities toward traditional securities fraud, including accounting and financial reporting violations. The agency has reduced its emphasis on some other enforcement areas while establishing a dedicated financial reporting and accounting unit within its enforcement division. The unit is intended to develop cases involving accounting practices, auditing and corporate financial disclosures. The existence of an inquiry involving Nvidia does not establish that the company misstated its financial results or violated securities laws. SEC investigators have not publicly identified any transactions, reporting periods or accounting standards under examination. The latest investigation has intensified selling pressure on Nvidia following a series of disclosures involving its former chief executive, export-control compliance and corporate transactions. The company lost more than a third of its market value during the broader crisis, with the latest weekly decline representing approximately $1 tn in lost capitalization. Nvidia’s Friday sell-off also affected the personal wealth of Jensen Huang. According to Forbes, Huang lost another $17.3 bn on November 20, reducing his estimated net worth to $110.2 bn and placing him 17th on its global billionaires ranking. His estimated fortune has declined by more than 25% since November 9, the first trading session following his public acknowledgment of the affair. The immediate question for Nvidia investors is whether the SEC’s confidential accounting inquiry develops into a formal enforcement case. The regulator has disclosed neither its specific concerns nor a timetable, leaving the investigation’s potential financial and legal consequences undetermined. title: Nvidia Stock Is Down 35% From Its High. History Suggests a $5,000 Investment Now Will Be Worth This Much by 2028. - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia has had a rough few days, but the future is still bright. Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock has gotten slammed over the past few weeks. With former CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang resigning from his position, the market has grown uncertain about Nvidia's future. Furthermore, some of Nvidia's practices have drawn increased scrutiny, which is also adding to fears. After the sell-off, Nvidia is down over 35% from its all-time high. Since the AI arms race kicked off in 2023, this is now the deepest sell-off Nvidia has seen, just surpassing the tariff-fear sell-off in April 2025. The market has made its opinion known, but does Nvidia actually deserve to be sold off this much? Or is this a generational buying opportunity? Let's take a look at where the stock could be by 2028, and if now is the perfect time to buy. With Nvidia's sell-off, it's now down over $2 trillion from its all-time high market cap. So, is Jensen Huang really worth $2 trillion to Nvidia's market cap? I think the market has way overblown this sell-off. Nvidia’s visionary leader definitely helped shape and drive the company. However, there are still thousands of employees who run the day-to-day operations and designs that Huang had nothing to do with. The real risk is if these employees start to quit or resign from their roles and that knowledge is lost. If there is a mass exodus from Nvidia alongside Huang, that could represent a huge risk for investors. Until we're a few months past Huang's resignation, the market is likely to stay cautious, which is one reason why Nvidia's stock price is down. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Another is the future. Huang's vision for where AI computing and GPUs will go placed Nvidia in a leadership role in the AI build-out. That will have driven product development over the next couple of years, but what comes after that is unknown. This is where a new CEO will need to have a great technical mind and vision for what's coming next. The wrong person at the helm could cause Nvidia's leadership position to collapse in the future if they cannot replicate Huang’s success. As a result, the market is once again discounting the stock until a new leader is selected. Lastly, there are concerns that Nvidia’s chips are potentially circumventing export restrictions to China, with some restricted products funneled through Southeast Asian countries, before eventually making their way into China. These are all allegations right now, but Nvidia hasn't been cleared of any wrongdoing yet, so once again, the market is discounting the stock. Nvidia has a lot of unknowns right now, and the market has kept it in a low-valued spot as a result. The question is, if these are resolved, what could it be worth? Nvidia has guided for 75% revenue growth in fiscal year (FY) 2028 (ending January 2028), thanks to the strength of the AI build-out. That's up from the 70% guidance given last quarter. With Nvidia estimated to generate around $424 billion in revenue this year, that would indicate revenue of $742 billion next year. At Nvidia's 62% profit margin, the company would generate $460 billion in profits. Even if the stock traded at the same trailing earnings multiple it does now, that would give it a market cap of $7.4 trillion -- more than doubling today's levels and turning $5,000 into at least $10,000. However, I think that is a dirt cheap price tag in and of itself, and most of Nvidia's problems will be solved by the end of next year. As a result, the market could value it like any other big tech stock and price it around 20 to 25 times earnings. That would result in an even larger market cap and make Nvidia a no-brainer buy today. title: Here's How Much Nvidia Stock Is Worth Without Jensen Huang, According to Dan Ives - The Motley Fool
content: Dan Ives revised his price target on Nvidia stock following Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO. Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) has experienced a stunning reversal following founder Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation amid controversy surrounding alleged connections to Chinese intelligence. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the semiconductor behemoth can maintain its technological edge without the executive who spent more than three decades building the company. Those concerns have contributed to a dramatic sell-off, even as Nvidia continues reporting ridiculously good financial results. The magnitude of the decline is anything but trivial. Nvidia stock reached a record closing price of around $239 in early October but has fallen to roughly $136 as of Nov. 20. That represents a decline of roughly 43%, wiping out more than $2.5 trillion in market capitalization and pushing Nvidia from the world's most valuable public company to fourth place. Nevertheless, Wall Street analyst Dan Ives thinks investors are overlooking Nvidia's underlying earnings power. Although he acknowledges that Huang's departure changes the company's investment thesis, his revised price target suggests meaningful upside remains. Ives has been particularly vocal about the consequences of Huang's resignation. During a recent interview, he estimated that Huang contributed $1 trillion to Nvidia's valuation. In a separate appearance, Ives described Huang as the company's "heart and lungs," emphasizing his influence over Nvidia's technological roadmap and competitive position. Ives says Nvidia stock is worth $225 without Huang and $300 with him as CEO. These figures provide an interesting way to quantify the so-called Jensen premium. The difference between Ives' two valuations is $75 per share, representing a 25% reduction from his original $300 target. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. If you’d invested $5,000 then, you’d be sitting on $1,631,761 today.* Now, for the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. It’s a key player in the $1.8 trillion space race, and with the stock recently sitting 20% off its highs, the window to get in early is closing fast. The implied difference in market capitalization is actually considerably larger than the $1 trillion Ives alluded to. With approximately 24.2 billion shares outstanding, a $75 difference translates into roughly $1.8 trillion in equity value. At Ives' respective price targets, Nvidia would command a market capitalization of approximately $7.3 trillion with Huang and $5.4 trillion without him. The difference in valuation illustrates the enormous importance Wall Street places on Nvidia's founder and why investors have reacted so negatively to his departure. Huang's value extends beyond his responsibilities as CEO. Since co-founding Nvidia in 1993, he has overseen the company's transformation from a graphics processing company into the dominant supplier of accelerated computing infrastructure. His investments in GPUs, CUDA software, and AI computing helped position Nvidia at the center of the technology industry's most important transformation since the birth of the internet. Perhaps Huang's greatest contribution has been leading Nvidia's culture of innovation. Huang consistently anticipated computing trends years before they became commercially relevant. This enabled Nvidia to develop new chip architectures and software ecosystems that competitors have struggled to replicate. This foresight helps establish durable competitive advantages and contributes to the company's pricing power. Huang also cultivated relationships with other technology executives, hyperscalers, governments, and AI labs. These supply chain connections have become important as Nvidia participates in data center build-outs that require complex financing arrangements and long-term strategic commitments. With all of that said, Nvidia's competitive advantages are not going to disappear just because Huang stepped away. The company's hardware and software ecosystem, engineering workforce, customer relationships, and product roadmap remain intact. Moreover, Ives acknowledges that Nvidia has a lead of two to three years over its competitors in AI chip technology. Although Huang's departure could narrow that advantage over time, the company's existing leadership provides a robust foundation for future growth. Despite reducing his Nvidia price target from $300 to $225, Ives maintains a bullish outlook on the company. At approximately $136 per share, his revised target implies roughly 65% upside, while his original $300 estimate implies 121% potential appreciation. Importantly, Ives' optimism centers on the insatiable demand for AI computing infrastructure and Nvidia's technological advantages. Following the company's earnings report on Nov. 17, Ives wrote that the results answered a critical question: "Demand did not leave with him." The financial evidence supports that assessment. Nvidia generated $115.8 billion in fiscal third-quarter revenue, representing 103% growth year over year, while data center revenue surged 110% to $107.6 billion. The company also reported a gross margin of 74.8%, demonstrating that its pricing power remains strong. Furthermore, Nvidia forecast $130 billion in revenue for the fourth quarter and raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to 75%. This forecast suggests the company is poised for further expansion despite the leadership transition. The central takeaway from Ives' analysis is that Nvidia doesn't necessarily need Huang to remain an attractive investment. Although his departure has reduced -- for now -- the premium investors are willing to pay, his price target still suggests considerable appreciation over the coming year. For investors who can stomach short-term volatility, Nvidia's recent sell-off could represent an opportunity to buy the dip in the most dominant AI infrastructure business at a significantly discounted valuation. title: Prediction: Nvidia Stock Will Do This in the 6 Months After a New CEO Takes Over, According to History - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia is searching for a new CEO following Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation. Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) is navigating one of the most consequential leadership transitions in recent Silicon Valley history. Following founder Jensen Huang's unexpected resignation amid a controversy involving alleged connections to Chinese intelligence, investors are growing increasingly concerned about the company's future. This uncertainty is weighing heavily on Nvidia stock, even as its underlying business continues to deliver extraordinary financial results. Colette Kress, Nvidia's former chief financial officer, is now serving as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. According to reports, the company is considering external candidates, including Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. History offers some clues about how technology stocks behave following major CEO transitions. However, Nvidia's circumstances are quite different from those of its peers, making the company's financial outlook particularly important right now. Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) represents a successful example of a technology leadership transition. Satya Nadella became CEO on Feb. 4, 2014, replacing Steve Ballmer after Microsoft conducted a formal succession search. Nadella had previously led Microsoft's cloud and enterprise businesses, giving him extensive knowledge of the company's operations. Microsoft stock advanced roughly 19% during Nadella's first six months as CEO. Of course, over the long term, he helped transform the Windows developer into a cloud computing powerhouse. Alphabet (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%) offers another example. Sundar Pichai became CEO of Alphabet on Dec. 3, 2019, succeeding co-founder Larry Page. However, Pichai had already served as Google's CEO since 2015, making the transition more of a consolidation of leadership responsibilities than an unexpected management overhaul. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Alphabet stock was higher roughly six months later, despite experiencing a meaningful drawdown during the short-lived COVID-19 market crash. Moreover, Page and his co-founder Sergey Brin remained involved as shareholders and directors, providing continuity that Nvidia currently lacks. Amazon (AMZN -4.10%) experienced a different outcome when Andy Jassy succeeded Jeff Bezos on July 5, 2021. Jassy was another internal executive who had previously built and led Amazon Web Services (AWS). Although Bezos relinquished the CEO position, he remains executive chairman, preserving his influence over the company's long-term strategy. Amazon shares declined approximately 6% during Jassy's first six months as CEO. At the time, investors were assessing the impacts of slowing pandemic-era growth and rising operating expenses on Amazon's e-commerce marketplace. The three examples above show that CEO succession can bring different short-term outcomes. However, they also share an important characteristic: Each of these companies promoted an experienced internal executive through an orderly transition, unlike Nvidia's abrupt leadership disruption. Nvidia's situation is unusual because Huang wasn't just another corporate executive. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and spent more than three decades directing the company's evolution from a graphics chip manufacturer into the world's leading supplier of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure. His influence extended across engineering, product development, corporate culture, and customer relationships. As a result of his departure, investors are increasingly questioning whether Nvidia can maintain its technological edge without the executive who helped establish it. The uncertainty is compounded by growing competition from custom AI accelerators developed by Alphabet, Amazon, and other hyperscalers. Nvidia's next CEO needs to prove they can preserve the company's innovation-driven culture while navigating complicated supply chains and regulatory relationships. Despite the unusual circumstances, Nvidia's financial outlook provides a compelling reason to anticipate a meaningful recovery. During its fiscal third-quarter earnings call, management increased its fiscal 2028 revenue growth forecast to 75%, up from its previous outlook of 70%. This suggests demand for Nvidia's accelerated computing platforms remains strong despite Huang's departure. Furthermore, Nvidia expects to generate $130 billion in revenue during the fourth quarter -- representing 91% growth year over year. The company is also forecasting gross margins of between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028, suggesting that accelerating sales growth will translate into additional profits. Nvidia's share repurchase program provides another subtle catalyst for the stock. In September, the board increased the company's existing authorization by $150 billion, leaving approximately $227.3 billion available at the end of the third quarter. Management intends to execute the remaining authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. By reducing the number of outstanding shares, stock buybacks can increase earnings per share (EPS) even if net income is unchanged. Combined with Nvidia's revenue growth and profit margins, upcoming share repurchases should fuel substantial EPS expansion over the coming year. My prediction is that Nvidia stock will trade higher six months after its new CEO assumes the role. The appointment itself should remove the primary source of uncertainty around the company, allowing investors to concentrate once again on revenue growth, earnings power, and competitive advantages. Although Burry claimed he "didn't say short" any of these companies, he maintains that he "provided the information one would need to sell." And Burry doesn't seem to see a bottom for the tech market anytime soon. In another X post, he compared today's market volatility to historic crashes in 1929 and 2000. Burry's primary reason for this correlation is "the lack of a proximate cause in earnings." On Substack, Burry expanded on this point, admitting that, although today's market leaders are "killing it with respect to earnings," that's no reason to expect higher prices. He cited articles from 1929 and 2000 to show how investors were in "complete shock that stocks were falling despite good news in earnings." Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock is down 7.5% as of 12:28 p.m. ET on Friday, Nov. 20, after the Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) IPO failed to revive the AI trade. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) and the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) are down 2.2% and 3.6%, respectively. Stocks stumbled around the world after the record IPO of the AI company Anthropic failed to restore investors' faith in AI -- an industry vital to the overall market, with 49% of the S&P 500 directly linked. AI stocks have had a tough go for some time now, with concerns over ballooning costs and limited value realized outside of specific applications -- namely, coding. Many investors were looking to the Anthropic IPO as a sort of "shot-in-the-arm" for AI stocks. But after opening yesterday 34% over the offer price of $83, Anthropic shares have fallen 25% from their high, now hovering just above the IPO price. Of course, Nvidia specifically has been dealing with fallout from the departure of its co-founder and 33-year CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12 in the wake of allegations of extramarital affairs, one of which was with a possible Chinese intelligence asset. The stock is headed for its seventh straight losing day, down 26% since the reports first surfaced. That's despite reporting another round of incredible numbers for its latest quarter, with sales jumping 103% year over year. title: Nvidia Stock NVDA Risks Breakdown Below $140 Support as CEO Search and SEC Probe Weigh - FXLeaders
content: NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) is trading at $141.64, down about -3.0%. The stock saw -3.30% fall yesterday and extended its losing streak to 6 sessions. The decline came after California’s attorney general issued a subpoena to the company and Anthropic’s debut failed to lift AI trade. Today, the market cap of NVDA is at $3.42 T. In its Q3 report, NVIDIA reported a year-over-year gain in revenue of about +103% with $115.8 B in that quarter. However, the analysts expectations were $109.1 B for the Q3 revenue. EPS also beat the analysts forecast of $2.48 and came in as $2.68 with +111% surge. As for profit, GAAP Net-Income came in at $65.3 B. The gross margin was also reported as 74.8%, which is up 1.4 points from previous year. Meanwhile, Data Center revenue rose +110% to $107.6 B, which is 93% of the total revenue. Given these numbers, it is clear that NVDA has a strong demand in market and is performing well across main parts of business. Another positive surprise was the Q4 outlook. The company expects the Q4 revenue around $130 B. Meanwhile, the Wall Street analysts anticipation sits at $125.1 B. However, the guidance does not include any Data Center compute revenue from China. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on 12th Nov and CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO. The board said it does not intend to reinstate Huang, and it is searching for a permanent CEO. On the other hand, California’s attorney general subpoenaed the company over whether its chips reached China, and the SEC is reportedly investigating, which added some selling pressure on stock. Another concern is that customers owed NVIDIA $81 B at the end of the quarter, which is about 64 days of sales. Any payment delay could hit price movement quickly. On valuation side, NVDA trades at a trailing P/E of 16 and a forward P/E at 10. The average Wall Street analysts consensus rating is Buy for the stock with 3 Strong Buy, 43 Buy, and 15 Hold ratings. The average price target by them is $224.50. Currently, the price target by Freedom Broker was lowered to $230 from $305. Whereas, William Blair downgraded the stock to Market Perform and RBC maintained its Outperform rating with a price target of $230. NVDA is trading below its 20-D moving average of $189 and its 200-D average of $204. The stock briefly slipped below $140 to about $138.90 after the open before bouncing, so the initial support remains at $140 level with the next support S2 at $135 level. On the upside, initial resistance lies at $145.98, with the longer term resistance point at $158.13. Any close above $145.98 could keep NVDA moving toward $150.96. On the other hand, any close below $140 could drag the price towards $135. For now, investors are focusing on the CEO search and the regulatory probes. NVIDIA stock is falling amid CEO uncertainty, regulatory probes by California’s attorney general and the SEC, and continued weakness in the broader AI trade. Wall Street analysts have an average price target of $224.50, with a consensus Buy rating. However, some analysts have recently lowered their targets or downgraded the stock. NVIDIA delivered strong Q3 results and issued better-than-expected Q4 revenue guidance. However, CEO uncertainty, regulatory investigations, and concerns about customer payments are weighing on investor sentiment. The $140 support level is important to watch, while $145.98 is the first resistance. A break below $140 could expose NVDA to further downside toward $135.

title: Does Huang’s Exit Sink Nvidia Stock? History Is Split - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? Nvidia’s board said on Tuesday’s earnings call that it does not intend to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO. Huang, the company’s co-founder, resigned with immediate effect on Nov 12. Most readers want to know who can run Nvidia without him. This article asks a different question. What happened to stocks when a founder left a market leader? The record gives no single answer. Our price data covers three founder-CEO exits at market leaders. A year later, Microsoft was down 48.0%. Apple was up 76.1%. Amazon was down 10.5%. Only Apple beat SPY, a fund that tracks the S&P 500, over one year and over three years. Here is how Nvidia has traded since the news. Nvidia fell 16.0% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. The Nov 11 close was the last one before Huang resigned. Over the same days, Broadcom rose 0.4%. SPY fell 5.8%. On Nov 12, the day of the announcement, Nvidia fell 4.3%. Advanced Micro Devices rose 5.9% that day. Broadcom rose 5.5%. On day one, money left Nvidia while two other big chip makers rose. The board’s statement came on the evening of Tuesday, Nov 17. The results release went out at 4:20 pm, after the close. From the Nov 17 close to the Nov 19 close, Nvidia fell another 6.1%. Broadcom rose 1.5%. AMD fell 2.8%, and SPY fell 2.3%. Nvidia is down 16.0% since the last close before Huang resigned, and 6.1% since the board said he would not return. If Nvidia is a big part of your savings, a drop like that is hard to sit through without wanting to sell. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s. See how it held up. One way to check is operating margin. That is the share of each dollar of sales left after the costs of running the business. The table below shows each founder exit, the stock’s return against SPY, and the margin before and after. Source: Intrinio split-adjusted closing prices and Morningstar income statements. Returns are price only. They run from the last close before the news to the close 252 trading sessions (one year) and 756 sessions (three years) later. SPY is measured over the same sessions. Margins compare the last full fiscal year before the exit with the third full fiscal year after it. Microsoft’s margin fell from 50.9% to 41.1%. Its stock lost 51.4% over three years. Apple’s margin went from 28.2% to 28.7%. Its stock rose 87.2% over three years. Amazon breaks the pattern. Its margin rose from 5.9% to 10.8%. Yet its stock trailed SPY over one year and over three years. Three cases are too few to make a rule. We read them as examples, not odds. Nvidia’s case also differs from all three. Bill Gates handed the job to Steve Ballmer and stayed on as chairman. Steve Jobs became Apple’s chairman when he gave up the CEO job. Jeff Bezos said ahead of time that he would step down, and he stayed on as executive chair. Huang left with immediate effect and also left the board. The chief financial officer agreed to serve as interim CEO. Nvidia’s operating margin was 66.9% in the quarter to Oct 25, 2026. That was the last full quarter before Huang left. Revenue was $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier. The company’s guidance for its fourth quarter implies a GAAP operating margin of about 63.0%. That would be lower than the third quarter. In their latest reported quarters, AMD’s margin was 21.2% and Broadcom’s was 54.3%. We think the margin is the better test of Nvidia after Huang, though it is not a sure one. At Microsoft, the founder’s exit came with a falling margin. At Apple, the margin held. At Amazon, the margin rose, but the stock still trailed SPY. For the earnings case, see Why Huang’s Exit May Not Sink Nvidia Stock. Nvidia was already 27.4% below its Oct 6 record close before Huang resigned. At Thursday’s close, it was 39.0% below that record. Much of the fall came before the CEO news. The wider market also fell. SPY fell 2.0% on Thursday, Nov 19. AMD fell 11.5% from the Nov 11 close to the Nov 19 close. No company statement or filing says how much of Nvidia’s fall is about Huang. We cannot split it from the wider market’s fall. Nvidia has been this far below a high before. After first closing a third below its Nov 2021 high, it fell another 49.7% to a low in Oct 2022. It closed back at its Nov 2021 high on May 25, 2023. That was a different time, and past falls do not set the path of this one. This question is part of our coverage of the AI story. Our read: a founder leaving has not decided where a market leader’s stock went. We would watch whether Nvidia’s margin holds up. Until it settles, owners may face more drops like this week’s. Those drops are easier to sit through when the rest of your money falls less than the market does. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. title: Prediction: Nvidia Will Hit a New All-Time High in 2027 (Hint: Watch This Metric) - The Motley Fool
content: Nvidia has lost nearly 37% of its market value in recent weeks, but an epic recovery could be in store next year. It's been a turbulent November for Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) as the company deals with the unexpected resignation of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. Uncertainty surrounding the company's leadership transition, investigations involving ties to China, and questions about its artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure partnerships are weighing heavily on investor sentiment. Nevertheless, Nvidia's latest financial results suggest the company's business is expanding at a record pace. During its fiscal third quarter (ended Oct. 25), Nvidia generated $115.8 billion in revenue, representing 103% year-over-year growth. Meanwhile, adjusted earnings per share (EPS) climbed 111% to $2.68. Despite this impressive performance, Nvidia stock is trading roughly 37% below its all-time high. With that said, one financial metric could ultimately drive the stock to new highs: earnings per share (EPS). Nvidia has two opportunities to expand EPS over the coming year, combining organic profit growth with an enormous share repurchase program. Nvidia's first opportunity to increase EPS comes directly from its underlying business. The company is a key beneficiary of AI-driven demand from hyperscalers expanding their data center build-outs. Nvidia's data center division generated $107.6 billion in revenue during the third quarter, increasing 110% year over year. What's particularly impressive is Nvidia's ability to convert its top-line growth into substantial profits. During the third quarter, the company reported a gross margin of 74.8%. This reflects the pricing power associated with Nvidia's GPUs, networking products, and CUDA software ecosystem. These economics allow Nvidia to generate enormous profits alongside an accelerating revenue base. Although management expects gross margin to moderate to between 71% and 72% in the fourth quarter, it anticipates a recovery to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028. More importantly, interim CEO Colette Kress raised the company's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to approximately 75% year over year, up from its previous projection of 70%. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Even if gross margin remains below its peak, Nvidia can still produce higher earnings through increased sales volumes and operating leverage. In other words, as revenue grows, certain operating expenses may increase at a slower rate relative to sales. This would allow additional revenue to contribute disproportionately to operating profits. The idea here is that Nvidia doesn't necessarily need to maintain record gross margins to achieve record earnings. Nvidia's second earnings catalyst is its share repurchase authorization. In September, Nvidia's board of directors approved a $150 billion increase to its existing repurchase program. As of the end of the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia had $227.3 billion remaining under its authorization. Management affirmed its intention to execute the remaining portion of the repurchase authorization by the end of fiscal 2028. This makes stock buybacks an important, albeit underrated, component of Nvidia's capital allocation strategy. The significance of Nvidia's share repurchases becomes clearer once you understand how EPS is calculated. Earnings per share equals a company's net income divided by its shares outstanding. When Nvidia repurchases and retires shares, the company effectively reduces the denominator in that equation. This means EPS can increase even if net income remains unchanged. For example, suppose a company generates $100 billion in annual net income across 25 billion shares. That would translate into EPS of $4.00. If the same company reduced its share count by 5%, while net income remained unchanged, EPS would increase to $4.21 without any additional revenue or profit growth. Stock prices are influenced by two interconnected variables: earnings per share and the valuation multiple investors are willing to pay for those earnings. A company's share price can rise even when its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio remains unchanged, provided EPS increases. This unique relationship makes the mechanics around Nvidia's potential earnings expansion particularly interesting. Nvidia's combination of projected revenue growth, compounding profitability, and aggressive share repurchases creates a compelling outlook around next year's EPS. These catalysts provide the foundation for a bounceback in Nvidia stock even without assuming a dramatic increase in the company's valuation multiple. I think Nvidia stock could soar next year, driven by accelerating EPS growth rather than speculative enthusiasm. Against this backdrop, investors should monitor Nvidia's net income growth and changes in shares outstanding over the coming quarters. Taken together, these metrics could reveal whether Nvidia's financial performance is strong enough to overcome its recent challenges and propel the stock to new highs. Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » AMD has been viewed as the No. 2 graphics processing unit (GPU) chipmaker for several years, with Nvidia comfortably holding on to the top spot. However, Nvidia suddenly faces significant uncertainty with former CEO Jensen Huang out of the company and angling for a comeback. Nvidia currently doesn't seem receptive to a reunion, and that can cost the company. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained. The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives. This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform. Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them. Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost. AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins. AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. Some investors argue that Huang's departure will make it difficult for Nvidia to continue innovating despite the competitive edge it has already obtained. The AI industry is moving rapidly, and leadership complexities can cost Nvidia valuable time. It can be the difference between missing out on the latest technology and watching hyperscalers turn to alternatives. This scenario positions AMD as the chipmaker with the most to gain from the confusion, and the company has been taking major steps to close the gap. For instance, AMD is making its chip fleet more attractive by making it much easier for developers to port existing Nvidia CUDA applications to its HIP platform. Nvidia's CUDA was previously a major moat. Moving to another software essentially meant rewriting vast amounts of code, but that's no longer the case. If AMD can win over more businesses with an easier migration, it creates more headaches for a company already full of them. Although Nvidia has captured most of the headlines throughout the AI boom, AMD has been quietly accelerating its growth. Data center revenue surged by 97% year over year in the third quarter, while overall revenue reached $13.4 billion, up by 45% year over year. That also represents a 16% sequential boost. AMD CEO Lisa Su told investors that demand for its AI products is still accelerating. The chipmaker also remains confident that revenue growth will surge in the coming years, along with higher net profit margins. AMD trades at a 30 forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which may be higher than what some investors are willing to handle. However, this same company almost doubled its net income year over year. AMD wrapped up the quarter with an 18.2% net profit margin, and if it can get closer to Nvidia's 62% net profit margin, the stock should have an easy time reclaiming a $1 trillion market cap and marching toward new highs.
